title: Peace with God; Adam and Christ
summary: Justified through faith, believers have peace with God, access to his grace, and a hope that suffering strengthens rather than destroys, because God has poured his love into their hearts by the Spirit. God proved that love when Christ died for the ungodly, while they were still sinners and enemies. Paul then sets the whole human story in two figures: through Adam's one trespass sin and death reigned over all, and through Christ's one act of obedience grace reigns and brings eternal life.
story: Chapters 1-4 answered the question of how anyone can be right with God: by grace, through faith, as Abraham was. Chapter 5 opens a new section (chapters 5-8) that asks what life looks like for people who have been justified, and whether their hope is secure. The first half of the chapter answers with peace, hope, and the love of God shown at the cross. The second half steps back to the widest possible view, from the beginning of humanity in Genesis 2-3 to the end, and shows that Christ is not only the answer to individual sins but the head of a new humanity, undoing what went wrong in Adam. Chapter 6 will take up the obvious objection that follows from verse 20.
historical:
Paul's Jewish contemporaries also reflected on how Adam's sin affected his descendants. Jewish writings from around the end of the first century AD, such as 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, lament that Adam's sin brought death to all his children, while also stressing each person's own responsibility; one line in 2 Baruch says that each person has become his own Adam. Paul shares the conviction that death entered through Adam, but he adds that the effects of Adam's act are matched and overwhelmed by the effects of Christ's.

The verse's history of interpretation is itself important. The final phrase of verse 12, because all sinned, was rendered in the Latin Bible that Augustine used as in whom all sinned, and Augustine took this to mean that all humanity sinned in Adam. That reading shaped the Western doctrine of original sin. Most modern scholars, Catholic and Protestant, agree that the Greek means because, not in whom, though many still hold that the passage teaches humanity's real solidarity with Adam's sin.
cultural:
Peace and reconciliation were political words in the Roman world. The emperor Augustus had presented himself as the bringer of peace, the Pax Romana, and Roman coins and monuments celebrated it. Reconciliation (katallage) was the word for restoring relations between parties at war or estranged, including enemy nations. Paul uses both words for what God has done: it is God who reconciles his enemies, at his own cost, rather than a conqueror imposing terms. Access (prosagoge, verse 2) could describe being introduced into the presence of a king.

Verse 7 reflects ordinary ancient values. Greek and Roman literature praised those who died for a friend, a benefactor, or their city. Someone might dare to die for a good man, Paul concedes. What no one expected was to die for enemies. That is what makes Christ's death a demonstration of God's love.
literary: Verses 1-11 are built around the verb rejoice or boast (kauchaomai), which appears three times: in hope (verse 2), in sufferings (verse 3), and in God himself (verse 11). The chain of verses 3-4, suffering to perseverance to character to hope, is a climax, each word picking up the last. Verses 9-10 use the argument from the greater to the lesser, familiar in Jewish interpretation: if God did the harder thing (reconciling enemies), how much more will he do the easier (saving the reconciled). Verses 12-21 are a sustained comparison. Paul begins it in verse 12, breaks off to explain himself (verses 13-17), then completes it in verses 18-19. The phrase how much more recurs, because the comparison is never equal: grace always exceeds the trespass. The phrase one man appears repeatedly, holding the two figures side by side.

outline.t: Peace, access, and hope that does not disappoint
Christ died for the ungodly: God's love proved
Sin and death through one man
The gift is not like the trespass
Condemnation in Adam, life in Christ

doctrines.note: Sin entered through one man and death through sin, and death spread to all because all sinned. Christians describe the connection differently: Augustinian and Reformed traditions speak of inherited guilt or Adam as humanity's representative head; Eastern Orthodox tradition stresses inherited mortality and corruption rather than guilt. All agree that humanity shares a condition it cannot fix itself.

Christ died for the ungodly, and believers are justified by his blood and reconciled through the death of God's Son. The initiative is entirely God's, and it was taken while people were still enemies.

Believers rejoice in the hope of the glory of God, and that hope does not disappoint, because God's love has been poured into their hearts. Suffering, rather than disproving the hope, produces perseverance and character.
Adam is a pattern of the one to come. Humanity is understood in terms of two heads, Adam and Christ, and each person belongs to one or the other. Christ is the beginning of a renewed humanity.

words.note: Katallasso, to reconcile, to change enemies into friends. In Paul, God is always the one who reconciles and people are reconciled to him, never the reverse (compare 2 Corinthians 5:18-20). The barrier is removed from God's side, at God's cost.

Tupos, pattern, type, or impression. A tupos was the mark left by a blow or a seal, and so an example or model. Paul calls Adam a type of the one to come: his role as head of humanity prefigures Christ's, though with opposite results. This is one source of the Christian practice of typology.

Paraptoma, trespass, a false step, a falling aside from the path. It appears six times in verses 15-20. Paul uses it for Adam's act, set against Christ's one act of righteousness; in verse 14 he also calls Adam's sin a transgression (parabasis), the breaking of a known command.

Prosagoge, access or introduction. It pictures being brought into the presence of a king or into a sanctuary. Through Christ believers have been brought into the grace in which they now stand. Paul uses it again in Ephesians 2:18 for access to the Father.

christ: This chapter shows Christ as both the demonstration of God's love and the head of a new humanity. God did not wait for people to improve: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” The death that reconciles enemies is the death of God's own Son, so the cross is not a third party appeasing an angry God but God himself paying the cost of peace. In the second half, Christ is the second Adam. Where Adam disobeyed and brought condemnation and death to the many, Christ obeyed and brought justification and life. Genesis 3 is not the last word on the human race; Christ is. Paul returns to the Adam-Christ contrast in 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and 45-49, where Christ is the last Adam and the one who raises the dead.

hard.q: Is it fair for all humanity to be affected by one man's sin, and must Adam be a historical person?
hard.a:
Many readers find it unjust that Adam's act should bring death and condemnation to people who were not there. Christian traditions have responded in several ways. Some say humanity was really present in Adam, as a tree is in its seed. Others, especially in the Reformed tradition, say Adam acted as humanity's appointed representative, and point out that the same principle of representation is what allows Christ's obedience to count for others. Others emphasize that Paul immediately adds because all sinned: people share not only Adam's condition but his choice. Eastern Orthodox theology speaks of inherited mortality and corruption rather than inherited guilt. Paul's own emphasis is that the gift is not like the trespass; whatever the loss through Adam, grace abounds much more.

On Adam's historicity, Christians also differ. Many hold that Paul's argument depends on a real first man whose act had real effects, just as Christ is a real man. Others, taking Genesis 1-3 as a theological account shaped by ancient Near Eastern literary forms, argue that Paul's point about universal sin and Christ's remedy stands whether Adam is read as a historical individual, a representative head of an early human population, or a figure for humanity. The confession that all have sinned and that Christ alone is the remedy is shared across these views.

questions: Paul says suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope. Where have you seen that chain at work, or seen it break?
What does it change to know that God loved you and acted for you while you were still his enemy?
Paul describes grace as always exceeding sin, how much more. Where do you find it hardest to believe that grace is greater than what went wrong?
